decisions.reason: SOL keeps the meaning while making the opening natural English.
SOL keeps the five senses and their function without the unnecessary possessive.
SOL combines the darkness and limited-visibility details from the adjacent baseline paragraph without changing the image.
The limited-visibility detail is retained in the merged paragraph.
SOL keeps the causal link between martial improvement and sharper senses in more natural prose.
The source says a single word was enough; SOL changes that into a claim about what the narrator had to say.
SOL keeps the same reaction; “in an instant” is unnecessary.
SOL preserves that they noticed the anomaly and spoke in turn, while keeping the timing.
The source refers to Jeok Cheongang’s suspicion in the singular.
The singular “suspicion” matches the source and keeps the ominous tone.
SOL keeps the ground vibration drawing closer in concise, natural prose.
SOL retains the comparison with the pursuers fought three times; the recast is natural.
“Strained my senses” keeps the effort to intensify perception and reads naturally.
The source describes intermittent impacts, not merely occasional heavier sounds.
SOL drops the timing that the chill came at the moment he realized what the sound was.
The statement is retained in the next paragraph, so the deletion loses no meaning.
SOL incorporates the human-made-sound contrast from the preceding paragraph and preserves the cursed monsters.
SOL keeps the approaching boom and the darkness and stench covering the hill.
The fragment “A monster” preserves the narrator’s correction in natural prose.
SOL preserves the three thousand witnesses freezing at the sight.
“Even” makes the source’s emphatic list structure clear and keeps the steel-hard loyalty image.
“Weathered” naturally preserves their experience of hardship.
“Refining” keeps the sense of cultivating their minds and bodies.
SOL retains both the futility of martial skill and experience and the shock’s force, consolidating the next sentence.
The shock overwhelming skill, age, and experience is retained in the merged paragraph.
SOL drops the source’s emphatic second beat: it was only natural.
SOL keeps the same shared reaction to the monster appearing atop the hill.
The lost-measurements image is retained in the next paragraph.
SOL keeps the overwhelming sight, the nearly twenty-foot height, and the tree-sized torso.
The em dash keeps the correction that the vast hole is the monster’s mouth.
SOL keeps the unnervingly slow cry and the wind carrying more than a stench.
SOL retains the naming of the power as Fear; the omitted transition does not change the sense.
The people’s ability to feel it is retained in the next paragraph.
The trembling air and hazy vision are retained in the next paragraph.
SOL preserves all three physical effects and joins them into a complete sentence.
SOL preserves the Daoist’s groan speaking for everyone.
SOL combines the question about describing the monster with the following question about the god’s permission.
The question about the god allowing the monster is retained in the merged paragraph.
“Inspired this much terror” naturally preserves the comparison with the followers of Dark Heaven.
The surviving human shapes are retained in the next paragraph.
SOL preserves both the human shape and the trace of the creatures’ original form.
“Towering over the hill” naturally conveys the monster standing high above it.
The conditional and uncertainty about Pangu’s existence remain intact.
SOL drops the detail that Pangu’s myth was passed down by hearsay alone.
SOL removes the monster as the subject of the footfall and drops the explicit link between its heavy step and the terror.
The fear of the unprecedented is retained in the next paragraph.
SOL preserves the suffocating fear and invisible-hand image while incorporating the preceding fear sentence.
The source says the feared outcome surely would have happened without the flash; SOL weakens this to “might have.”
SOL drops the source’s explicit instant timing as the darkness splits.
The source identifies the deep-blue phenomenon as flame; SOL changes its category to energy.
The fragment “Fire” keeps the reveal and works naturally after the preceding description.
SOL keeps the hellfire’s light, darkness, and destructive power.
“Far end” changes the fire’s specified tip into a less precise location.
The roar shaking the air is retained in the merged paragraph.
SOL combines the roar and the arm’s swing without losing either event.
The image of the man and spear as one is a natural rendering of the source’s fused-together image.
The source describes a sound of air splitting; SOL changes it into the fist itself tearing through the air.
SOL drops the forceful fist bearing down on Jin Taekyung, an important part of the action.
“Deep-blue” preserves the flame’s color, and the tighter phrasing keeps his stride and spearhead unwavering.
SOL incorporates the heat-warped space and fire-dragon image from the following paragraph.
The heat and fire-dragon image are retained in the preceding merged paragraph.
“A spear form” naturally preserves the named technique as a form devised by an ancestor of the Fire Gate Clan.
The fire-dragon tail still glides through the air and meets the monster’s fist.
The sharp cut heard by the onlookers is retained in the next paragraph.
SOL keeps both the sharp sound and the severed mass of flesh.
The monster seeing the severed fist is preserved without an unnecessary conjunction.
SOL keeps the monster’s puzzled look at the place where its fist had been.
“Surface” is less precise than the source’s freshly severed edge, where the blood begins to bead.
SOL preserves the delayed pain, unanswered question, and the monster’s incomprehension.
“Streaking” preserves the spearhead’s speed and its continued motion toward a single point.
SOL retains the simultaneous heat and cold while keeping the reaction concise.
The source specifies that the monster’s roar is cut off; SOL weakens it to a generic cry.
SOL adds that the man’s eyes are “unyielding,” an attitude not stated in the source.
“Low” preserves the voice’s sinking tone; “steady” is not required by the source.
SOL preserves the monster’s inability to understand and Jin’s reading of that fact in its eyes.
“That’s all you were allowed” keeps the sense that the monster’s capacity was limited.
The murmuring and troubled gaze are retained in the next paragraph.
SOL combines the murmuring and somber gaze with the monster’s fading eyes and Jin’s clenched jaw.
“Brought you into being” naturally preserves the question of who created the monster.
SOL clarifies that he was not asking the monster, without changing the source’s meaning.
SOL preserves the question aimed both at himself and at the emerging enemies.
SOL drops the source’s explicit intensity: the ground shook violently.
SOL preserves the faint vibrations beneath the nearer enemies’ noise and their layered arrival from all directions.
The large and small tremors are retained in the preceding paragraph; this line keeps the muttering beat.
The certainty is retained in the next paragraph’s opening.
SOL keeps the certainty and carefully planned encirclement in a smoother sentence.
SOL preserves that low-Intelligence monsters could not have formed this net on their own.
SOL keeps the bells carried on the wind from all around and Jin twisting the embedded spearhead.
SOL preserves the death, collapse, foul blood, and the blood soaking his collar.
“He didn’t care” keeps the meaning without the redundant intensifier.
SOL preserves the repeated bloodshed through the night and possibly for days afterward.
“The only way” preserves the source’s necessity: he must spill their blood to break through and head east.
“All they could do was fight” keeps the source’s only remaining course of action.
SOL preserves the low command and weapons leveled toward the enemy without adding “steady.”
